doc.title: Roy McCurdy interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995

title: Band style, pianists and the 'Big Man' show
summary: The band mixed funk, gospel and odd meters, with a roster of pianists; Black Messiah and the unfinished John Henry show.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: Did you have a name for it or did you let other people name it?

We just let other people name it. We just called it — it was just music for us you know. We didn’t want to be in one particular slot all the time, like just straight ahead jazz or something. We wanted to be able to do all kinds of things and have some fun. And not only did we do different like Funk and Soul and Gospel and Jazz, we also experimented with different time figures and things too at that time. Like seven-four time, five-four time and things like that, which were, we did “Seventy Four Miles Away” that album was seven-four time. And then George Duke came up with a tune in five-four that we did, it was great. He was one of the wonderful piano players that came through, Joe Zawinul, George Duke, Hal Galper, and then there was Mike Wolff came on the band, I don’t know if you know Mike. He was the musical director for the Arsenio Hall show. But he was our last piano player. Larry Willis was on the band for a while.
And he was with Blood, Sweat and Tears too wasn’t he, later on?
Yeah. Larry was, actually I think Larry recommended me for the job, because he was on there before me.
That one record you did, “Black Messiah” I think it was, there was some interesting stuff on that too. Music from that, didn’t they write a Broadway show? Called John Henry or something?

Yeah. But that was an album on a show we were working on called “Big Man” which was like about John Henry. And Cannon and Nat had written all the music for that. We recorded it actually. But before we could get the show off the ground, he passed away. Yeah, it was beautiful.
